subject: Followup to a mixture modeling question

messages.author: f769d7d2cfcf4edc
messages.subject: Followup to a mixture modeling question
parts:
Hey everyone (and Bob).

I had asked in a thread how to go about extracting class membership probabilities from a mixture.
I was doing so incorrectly.

Before, I had a likelihood with per-person membership weights; e.g.,: p(y_i | ...) = pi_{i1}*p(y_i | params_1) + (1 - pi_{i1})*p(y_i | params_2), and put a hierarchical prior on p_i, e.g., pi_i = logit(lambda_i); lambda_i ~ logistic(mu, sigma); mu ~ logistic(0,1); sigma ~ cauchy+(0,1).

Bob informed me this is not correct.
He told me instead the likelihood should be: p(y_i | ...) = pi_1*p(y_i | params_1) + (1 - pi_1)*p(y_i | params2); and one can obtain pi_{i1} post-hoc by: pi_{i1} = pi_1*p(y_i | params_1) / sum_{k=1}^2 (pi_ik * p(y_i | params_k))
This makes sense.
However, I want to predict pi_ik, and have the predictors better inform the clustering itself, such that an intercept-only model is basically going to be the same as just a clustering method, but more predictors informs cluster membership.

It seems like with the above method, one could extract individual probabilities, pi_ik, and regress them (deterministically) onto various predictors.

Is it possible to flip this, and parameterize solely in terms of pi_ik, then reconstruct pi_1 and pi_2 for the likelihood?

I gave it a shot, and I'm curious whether this would be a better way to go.

Here is my work:
http://imgur.com/a/LA8F8

I numbered in the order I derived everything.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Followup to a mixture modeling question
parts:
> On Feb 10, 2017, at 2:18 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hey everyone (and Bob).
>
> I had asked in a thread how to go about extracting class membership probabilities from a mixture.
> I was doing so incorrectly.
>
> Before, I had a likelihood with per-person membership weights; e.g.,: p(y_i | ...) = pi_{i1}*p(y_i | params_1) + (1 - pi_{i1})*p(y_i | params_2), and put a hierarchical prior on p_i, e.g., pi_i = logit(lambda_i); lambda_i ~ logistic(mu, sigma); mu ~ logistic(0,1); sigma ~ cauchy+(0,1).

If pi is supposed to be the mixing proportions, there's not a different pi
per outcome.

> Bob informed me this is not correct.
> He told me instead the likelihood should be: p(y_i | ...) = pi_1*p(y_i | params_1) + (1 - pi_1)*p(y_i | params2); and one can obtain pi_{i1} post-hoc by: pi_{i1} = pi_1*p(y_i | params_1) / sum_{k=1}^2 (pi_ik * p(y_i | params_k))


> This makes sense.

Not quite. There is no "pi[i, 1]" (that {i1} notaiton is suboptimal because we don't know if
that's one index "i1" or two indexes, "i" and "1".).

Instead, what you're doing is assuming a discrete parameter sequence z, taking, in
roughly your notation:

z[i] ~ bernoulli(pi);
y[i] ~ p(y[i] | params[z[i]]);

What you're calling "pi[i, 1]" is actually this

E[z[i] | y] = Pr[z[i] = 1 | y]

It's not some latent parameter or something. What we've done
is marginalized out the z and then we compute the expectation,
which turns out to be the probability that z is one given that
it's a binary variable.

> However, I want to predict pi_ik, and have the predictors better inform the clustering itself, such that an intercept-only model is basically going to be the same as just a clustering method, but more predictors informs cluster membership.

Then you need a different model where z[i] is instead of being
modeled as Bernoulli, is modeled with some kind of logistic
regression or something.

z[i] ~ bernoulli_logit(w[i] * gamma)

where w[i] is the predictor(s) for z[i] and gamma are the
coefficients for that logistic regression.

- Bob

Gotcha, ok. I find it interesting that my model still 'works' (it tends to correctly assign people to the right cluster; the estimated parameters are correct), but I think fixing this issue will result in a massive speed up, regardless.
By 'the parameters are correct', I mean the mixture distributions' parameters are correct, people are typically assigned to the correct cluster, and the prior weights are also still correct (N_1 = 300, N_2 = 200; p(K = 1 | ...) = .6), and this is using a per-person weight in the likelihood with a prior on the weights.  No idea why this works just fine after reading what you said. Of course, I fit a gaussian mixture using your method (with prediction too), and it also worked fine, but was much, much faster (and optimizing worked; optimizing doesn't work using my method).

Thanks for your response! Extremely helpful, as always.

messages.author: f769d7d2cfcf4edc
messages.subject: Re: Followup to a mixture modeling question
parts:
Just as yet another followup, it appears that our methods provide basically equivalent solutions.

Both work via optimizing, both provide nearly identical estimates for latent group membership betas, both adequately cluster individuals, etc.
It seems that when I add predictors, my method actually recovers latent group memberships more accurately for reasons I don't understand (my guess is that it allows more variability in pi_i's than deriving them from Pi_1 would permit).
Your method is faster than mine, but mine is easier to plug into another model of mine. (Because treating pi_i as a parameter directly is /much/ easier for a particular model of mine than would be treating pi_i as a derived quantity).
Seems like the big difference between the methods: 1) Yours treats pi_{i,1} as a derived quantity from Pi_1, where Pi_1 is the parameter 2) Mine treats pi_{i,1} as a parameter, and Pi_1 as a hyper parameter. Though it may not be mixture-modeling kosher, they provide the same estimates of the parameters and hyper parameters. Yours is faster, but less flexible for my usecase (where I have nested mixture models, and deriving pi_{i,1} would be incredibly difficult); mine takes longer to estimate (not by much, though, to be fair), but it can directly model pi_{i,1}. So it seems to be a different posterior, but provides the same inferences.

The posterior variances also differ in expected ways. Using your method, some error should manifest itself in the mixture components' parameters (not permitting individual clustering directly, so to speak, means the gaussian parameters are less certain), and as a result, the posterior SD of the mu's and sigma's is greater than in my method. On the other hand, my posterior SD of the Pi_1 estimate is larger than yours, because of the stochastic nature of individual pi_{i,1}'s presumed to be generated by a Pi_1 hyper parameter.

Interesting.
